title: An Expanded View of Complex Traits: From Polygenic to Omnigenic
authors: Boyle EA, Li YI, Pritchard JK
population: Published height GWAS summary statistics from the GIANT consortium, with replication effect sizes estimated in the Health and Retirement Study
funder: This work was supported by RO1 HG008140, the National Science Foundation graduate research fellowship program and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.
authorConflicts: No statement in the PMC author manuscript.
result: Perspective with new analysis. Fisher showed in 1918 that if many genes affect a trait, random sampling of alleles produces a continuous, normally distributed phenotype. Height illustrates the extreme polygenicity typical of many complex traits: across all SNPs genome-wide, the median SNP is associated with an effect of 0.14 mm on height, about one tenth of the median effect of genome-wide significant SNPs (1.43 mm). Under simplifying assumptions the authors estimate that more than 100,000 SNPs have independent causal effects on height. They propose an omnigenic model as a hypothesis.
